Only the retained snapshot's tests were searched; test files outside the captured tree are out of scope.

investigations.question: After a follower installs a snapshot whose index is below the follower's own cached last log index, which code reconciles the follower's cached/advertised last log position and its local log entries with the installed snapshot, and can the leader's back-off then repeat the same snapshot indefinitely?
investigations.hypothesis: installSnapshot never revises the cached last log index/term, while its sibling path restoreUserSnapshot explicitly does; since getLastEntry/getLastIndex prefer the snapshot only when the cached log index is below the snapshot index, a follower whose cached last index is above the installed snapshot keeps advertising and comparing against its own divergent log. With a divergence at or below the snapshot index (the condition that caused the snapshot) and a leader whose log no longer contains entries below its snapshot index, the pair repeats: InstallSnapshot(snapshotIndex) succeeds and sets nextIndex = snapshotIndex+1; the next AppendEntries carries PrevLogEntry = snapshotIndex and is rejected with NoRetryBackoff and LastLog = the follower's higher stale index; the leader clamps nextIndex back to snapshotIndex; the request for snapshotIndex-1 cannot be built from the leader's compacted log, so the same snapshot is sent again.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the follower's cached last log is lowered on install (or if the advertised/resp.LastLog is not the stale value), if the receiver can accept PrevLogEntry = snapshotIndex from the snapshot metadata alone, if the leader can always build a request for snapshotIndex-1 (log not compacted there), or if the cycle is broken by any other terminating condition such as a successful truncation. An executed witness would be a leader with a compacted prefix whose first index is snapshotIndex+1 and a follower whose log diverges at or below snapshotIndex while its cached last index is above it, then observing repeated InstallSnapshot requests instead of ForwardProgress.
limitations: Source-derived reachability argument with explicit conditions; no receipt, because this run had no experiment capacity left.

The reachability of 'cached last index above the installed snapshot index' is argued from a divergent-suffix history (a node that kept uncommitted entries from an earlier leader and whose index outran the leader's snapshot point); no execution confirms that history end to end.
Only the leader-to-follower snapshot path is examined; the user-initiated restore path is the sibling that does perform the update.

investigations.question: Do the retained snapshot-install tests exercise a follower whose cached last log index exceeds the installed snapshot index, and what do their premises fix as required behaviour?
investigations.hypothesis: Both tests create the snapshot path by disconnecting a follower and letting the leader advance, so the follower's cached last index stays below the snapshot index; the asserted requirement is convergence after reconnect, which the snapshot-preference route of getLastEntry/getLastIndex satisfies. Neither test constructs an index-ahead follower, so no retained expectation contradicts the recorded repeating-install cycle.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if either test manipulates a follower's log or cached last index so that it exceeds the snapshot index the leader will send, or if it asserts something about resp.LastLog/nextIndex across repeated installs. A passing suite over the index-behind case says nothing about the index-ahead case.
limitations: Coverage of two tests is not coverage of the product: the absence of a test is evidence about the retained material, not proof that the index-ahead case is unreachable or harmful.
No execution was performed (tests were read, not run).

investigations.question: How can a member reach the state the repeating-InstallSnapshot cycle requires - a cached last log index above the leader's newest snapshot index together with a divergence at or below that index - and which conditions prevent it?
investigations.hypothesis: The state is produced by an uncommitted suffix that survives on a minority node. A leader appends entries that only reach a minority, so a later leader can be elected by a majority whose logs do not contain them (the vote rule compares only the voters' own last term/index); the new leader's snapshot index is its FSM's applied index at snapshot time, which is bounded only by the committed configuration index, so the snapshot can sit below the old high-water mark. The minority node keeps its suffix because the only sustained truncation happens when a leader can send entries whose previous log entry matches (or whose terms conflict) at an index the leader still holds; a leader that has compacted past the divergence point cannot, and each InstallSnapshot only rewrites FSM state plus the region up to the snapshot index, leaving the divergent suffix and the cached last index alone.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the diverging suffix must be held by a majority (in which case the next leader's log necessarily contains it), if the new leader's snapshot index cannot fall below the old leader's last index, if snapshot installation removes or reconciles the divergent suffix in every store configuration, or if the leader can always build a request at the last shared index. An executed witness would be a node holding a superseded leader's uncommitted suffix longer than the current leader's snapshot index, with the leader's first log index above the divergence point, observed to keep receiving snapshots while its match index stays at the snapshot index.
limitations: Construction argued from retained code paths; not driven through a cluster, and no receipt exists (this run's experiment capacity was already consumed).
Requires the node to remain in the configuration and be reachable, and the leader's compaction to have passed the divergence point.
Store-specific behaviour (monotonic versus compacting stores) changes how the follower's log looks after install but not the advertised position that drives the cycle.

investigations.question: Which consensus RPC handlers decide whether the sender is eligible, and where does that decision sit relative to the term and authority effects each handler performs?
investigations.hypothesis: All five handlers are admitted through one dispatch path whose only common check is checkRPCHeader (protocol-version bounds). Inside the handlers the behaviour splits: requestVote and requestPreVote return early when the sender's ID is absent from the latest configuration, and they do so before the term-adoption branch, so a sender outside the configuration cannot even raise the receiver's term; appendEntries and installSnapshot have no such check and will adopt a higher term and record the sender as leader (installSnapshot additionally installs the configuration carried in the request), and timeoutNow performs its transition with no check at all. So the eligibility guard is absent from three of the five handlers, not unique to TimeoutNow, and the transfer finding must rest on the transfer-specific effect rather than on uniqueness of the omission.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if any of appendEntries, installSnapshot or timeoutNow consults the configuration (or another sender-authority condition) before its term/leader/transition effects, or if the vote handlers can adopt a term before rejecting an ineligible sender. A nonexistent-sender experiment would settle the non-member consequence, but the ordering question itself is decided by the handler bodies.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); the distribution is read from handler bodies, and the non-member consequence assumes transport reachability, which the RPC layer deliberately does not provide on its own.

A member that is not the leader can perform the same term/leader effects by sending an AppendEntries/InstallSnapshot with a higher term, so the distribution matters mainly for the non-member or stale-sender case.

investigations.question: Which configuration does a candidate evaluate its vote count against at the moment it declares leadership, and can that configuration change during the candidacy without ending it?
investigations.hypothesis: The required count is captured once, at the top of runCandidate, from configurations.latest at that instant; the win test inside the loop compares the accumulated grants against that captured value and never recomputes it, while nothing in the loop re-derives it when configurations.latest changes. Two receive-side paths can change configurations.latest while the node remains a Candidate: installSnapshot has no state guard (its own comment says it must only be called as a follower) and installs the request's configuration, and appendEntries skips the step-down for a candidate whose candidateFromLeadershipTransfer flag is set, so it can append a configuration entry to a still-campaigning node. Therefore a node can take leadership with a count that is below the majority of the configuration it holds at that moment.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if votesNeeded is recomputed (or the candidacy restarted) whenever configurations.latest changes during the loop, if installSnapshot rejects or is otherwise unreachable from a non-follower state at an equal term, if appendEntries ends every candidacy regardless of the transfer flag, or if the win test consults the configuration rather than the captured count. An executed witness would be a candidate that receives a configuration-growing message at its own term and then declares leadership with fewer grants than the majority of its new configuration.
limitations: Source-derived; no receipt exists (this run's experiment capacity was already consumed).

The direct claim is about the justification of the win (stale majority); the split-vote consequence is a conditional implication that additionally needs a same-term competitor whose votes are disjoint from the candidate's.

Whether an operator's deployment can produce a same-term competitor plus a configuration-growing message to a candidacy was not measured; only the code paths that permit the configuration change are established here.

investigations.question: Can the transport's heartbeat fast path, which runs a consensus handler on a connection goroutine, touch commit, log or configuration state that the main loop owns?
investigations.hypothesis: The fast path is admitted only for a request whose previous-log fields, entry list and leader commit index are all zero, and for those inputs the handler reduces to thread-safe mutations (atomic state/term, mutex-protected leader and last-contact fields), leaving commit advancement, log application and configuration reads on the main thread - so the arrangement the registration comment requires is satisfied and the guard is the admission test itself.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted by any request shape that reaches the fast path while carrying entries or a non-zero leader commit index, by any main-thread-owned read or write performed before those guards, or by the fast path being taken for the commit-index-only re-replication the replication loop sends on its CommitTimeout. A race-detector run over a large-cluster snapshot catch-up would be the executed form.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no race detector was run.
Covers the NetworkTransport path only; the in-memory test transport stores the handler without using it in its RPC path.

investigations.question: What does a receiver conclude from its durable vote record when the term and the candidate were written as two separate stable-store operations, and can that conclusion grant a vote it should have denied?
investigations.hypothesis: The vote record is two independent writes (term, then candidate) over an interface that offers only single-key operations, so a crash between them leaves a newer term paired with the previous term's candidate. The duplicate branch then grants on identity bytes alone when the stored term equals the request term, without the log up-to-dateness comparison that a first-time grant performs; the branch is therefore reachable for a term in which the node never actually granted anything, and its grant carries less evidence than the code path it replaces.
investigations.discriminator: Settled by (a) reading whether any supported StableStore or the surrounding code makes the term and candidate writes atomic, and (b) a crash-injection probe that interrupts the process between the two writes, restarts it, and observes the answer to a vote request at the newer term from the previous candidate while the node's own log has advanced past that candidate's. Refuted if the two writes are atomic in every supported store, if the duplicate branch is unreachable with a candidate from an older term, or if the grant carries the log comparison in a path not read here.
limitations: Source-only; no crash-injection or store inspection was performed (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted).
The interface shows only single-key operations; whether a particular deployment's store offers batching that this code could use was not examined beyond the captured tree.
The consequence needs a specific vote split as well as the crash window, so this record does not claim a reachable loss of a committed entry.

investigations.question: Which evidence makes the transfer path treat a named peer as up to date, and can that evidence exist without any successful exchange with that peer?
investigations.hypothesis: The only per-target condition before TimeoutNow is the catch-up loop over followerReplication.nextIndex, and that field is initialised optimistically to the leader's last index plus one whenever replication state is created (leader start and configuration changes) and is reduced only when a peer answers an AppendEntries with a rejection; a transport error increments the failure counter and returns without touching it. A peer that has been unreachable since that initialisation therefore satisfies the loop without a single successful exchange, and the automatic target choice compares the same field, so both the readiness test and the 'most up to date' choice rest on an uncorroborated estimate.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if nextIndex is ever seeded from the peer's reported position, if transport errors also reduce it, or if some other condition (a successful heartbeat, a stored match index, or the replica's own reported last index) gates the transfer. An executed witness would be a three-node cluster whose leader was elected while one voter was unreachable, followed immediately on that voter's return by LeadershipTransferToServer for it, observing TimeoutNow being sent before any successful AppendEntries response from that peer.
limitations: Source-only; the window was not measured, and the retained material does not say how long a peer can remain in the 'cursor above last index' state.
The condition is about evidence, not about a guaranteed bad outcome: a target whose log happens to be current still wins the induced election.
Only the transfer path and the automatic target choice were traced; other consumers of nextIndex were not re-examined.

investigations.question: Which statements in the captured design documents bear on configuration handling and non-voter participation, and do they contradict a recorded finding or convert one of my earlier suspicions into documented design?
investigations.hypothesis: The membership proposal says a new configuration is in effect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when committed), that at most one configuration may be uncommitted at a time, and that the latest configuration is almost always the one used - which is exactly the commitment behaviour I had considered as a possible progress defect; and it defines Voter versus Nonvoter by participation ('vote is counted in elections and whose match index is used in advancing the commit index' versus 'receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes'), which anchors the requirement behind the non-voter transfer finding. One proposal line about GetConfiguration does not match the shipped documentation, but the shipped documentation is the contract.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted as requirement support if the shipped code contradicts those statements without saying so (which would make the document current normative text rather than a proposal), and refuted as a negative if some recorded finding actually depends on a configuration taking effect only at commit; the GetConfiguration point is settled by the shipped doc comment.
limitations: membership.md is a review proposal written before the implementation, not a specification: it even labels its catch-up threshold a placeholder and describes AddVoter as staging-oriented, while the shipped code documents AddVoter as adding a voter and deprecates Staging. It is therefore used only where the shipped code and the API documentation agree with it.
Only the captured documents were read (docs/apply.md, docs/README.md and membership.md); no external specification was consulted, per the run's search restrictions.

investigations.question: Does any retained scenario combine a leadership transfer with a non-voting member, and can the randomized suite stand in for the explicit transfer API?
investigations.hypothesis: No. The fuzzy leadership-transfer scenario builds a five-node cluster with no non-voters, transfers three times with writes in between, and asserts log and FSM equality; the only retained test whose subject is non-voters demotes the sole peer of a two-node cluster and then calls the automatic transfer entry point, which fails during target selection before any TimeoutNow is sent. The explicit-target API is therefore never exercised against a non-voting member anywhere in the retained suite.

Reading the scenario bodies settles it; no execution is needed for a coverage claim.
limitations: A coverage claim, not a behavioural one: absence of a scenario is evidence about the retained material, not proof that the uncovered path is harmless or harmful.
Only the captured tree's tests and fuzzy scenarios were searched.

investigations.question: Do the retained randomized scenarios ever take a snapshot or reach the snapshot-send/install paths, so that their verifications could bear on the recorded snapshot-install cycle?
investigations.hypothesis: No. The fuzzy harness starts from the default configuration and then sets the snapshot threshold to a value far above the entry counts the scenarios generate and the snapshot interval to an hour, so no snapshot is created during a scenario run; with no snapshot the leader never compacts its log, so a node behind the head is always recovered by log transfer and the transport never sends an InstallSnapshot. The suite's verifications (single leader per term, log equality, FSM equality) therefore exercise consensus without the snapshot path.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if any fuzzy scenario takes a snapshot explicitly, lowers the threshold or interval, or restarts a node such that a snapshot is restored, or if the harness's partition scenarios force an install through log compaction rather than through an explicit snapshot. Reading the harness configuration and the scenarios settles it.
limitations: Coverage of the retained scenarios only; other harnesses outside the snapshot are out of scope.
This does not bear on the correctness of the snapshot path, only on whether the retained randomized evidence constrains it.

investigations.question: What does the retained convergence assertion compare, and what would it therefore have detected about a follower that keeps reinstalling a snapshot instead of making progress?
investigations.hypothesis: The assertion compares, between every node, the ordered slice of command payloads their FSM applied and the sequence of configurations their FSM recorded, retrying until a longstop timeout and then failing with a length or content mismatch. It compares no Raft-level state: not the log store, not applied/commit indexes, not replication cursors. So it would detect a stalled follower as a payload-length mismatch, but it would not detect a follower whose applied payloads happen to match while its log or cursor state does not.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the assertion also compares logs, indexes or cursors, or if the FSM it uses records something other than the applied payloads. Reading the helper and the FSM implementation settles it.
limitations: Coverage of the assertion only; it says nothing about whether the recorded cycle occurs.
The helper's sensitivity to a stall depends on the longstop timeout being long enough for the mismatch to appear within a test run.

investigations.question: Can the configuration-change admission condition flip from closed to open without the leader loop being woken, so that an accepted change request is never dispatched?
investigations.hypothesis: No, not through the leader's own paths. The condition reads the latest and committed configuration indexes and the current commit index; while the node is leader, appendConfigurationEntry writes the latest index from inside the loop, and the commit handler inside the same loop writes both the commit index and the committed configuration index. Commitment bookkeeping is advanced by replication goroutines but only feeds a notification channel that the loop consumes, so no input changes while the loop is not looking. The one receive-side path that can change the latest configuration index for a same-term node (appendEntries appending a configuration entry) is either irrelevant to a leader because it also transitions the node to follower, or applies to a transfer candidacy, which is not in the leader loop.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if any path can raise either the commit index or the latest configuration index of a running leader outside the leader loop, or if the helper is consulted only once per iteration in a way that skips re-evaluation after the commit handler runs. An executed witness would be an accepted configuration change whose future stays pending while the conditions are actually satisfied.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted).

The claim is about the leader's own paths and the receive-side paths that exist in the captured code; a future change that adds another writer of those fields would invalidate it, which is what the note itself warns about.

investigations.question: When a reload changes the election timeout, which running state adopts the new value, and what wakes it to do so?
investigations.hypothesis: The candidate loop has a branch that compares its current election timeout with the configured value and re-arms the timer when they differ, and that branch is woken by the follower notification channel, which the reload path signals only when the heartbeat timeout decreased. A reload that changes the election timeout without decreasing the heartbeat timeout therefore cannot reach the branch, so a running candidacy keeps the timer it started with, while the follower state does re-arm promptly through its own notification case.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the follower notification channel has another producer, if the candidate re-reads the election timeout on some other trigger (for example its own timer or a configuration read), or if the reload path's condition also covers a changed election timeout. An executed witness would be a candidate with a long configured election timeout, a reload that lowers only the election timeout, and observation of when the candidacy restarts.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no reload was exercised against a running candidate.

The reloadable-configuration documentation for this field states what it means, not when a change takes effect, so this is an implementation mismatch with the refresh branch's evident purpose rather than a violated written promise; the impact is bounded because the next candidacy reads the configured value at entry.
Only the two notification consumers and the reload notifier were traced.

investigations.question: When the instance is shut down while client requests have been queued but not yet processed, what resolves those requests' futures?
investigations.hypothesis: Nothing does. The main loop returns on shutdown without draining any request channel, so requests sitting in a buffered channel are never answered; the leader's cleanup only covers requests already moved to its inflight list; and the future type provides a shutdown escape only if the request carried a shutdown channel, which the user-facing request paths never set. With the documented option that buffers the apply channel, an apply or barrier future can therefore remain unresolved forever, and a verify future can do the same through its buffered channel.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if shutdown drains or rejects queued requests, if inflight cleanup reaches channel-queued requests, or if the user-facing enqueue paths arm the futures' shutdown channel. An executed witness would be: enqueue more applies than the loop can process with the buffering option enabled, shut the instance down, and observe futures whose Error() never returns.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no shutdown race was exercised.

The window depends on the option that buffers the apply channel and on timing: with the default unbuffered channel a request that was accepted has been received by the loop, which then either dispatches it (inflight cleanup covers it) or rejects it.
The record is about completion of client futures, not about durability or ordering of the entries involved.

investigations.question: What relationship must the leader-lease timeout have with the leader's own peer-contact cadence, and does the configuration validation enforce it?
investigations.hypothesis: The lease check declares a follower contacted when the elapsed time since its last response is at most the lease timeout, and the leader's periodic contact with a follower comes from a heartbeat at one tenth of the heartbeat timeout and a commit-timeout re-replication; the validation bounds the lease only to at least five milliseconds and at most the full heartbeat timeout, so a configuration with a small lease and a large heartbeat is accepted even though the lease is then shorter than the interval at which the leader is actually able to speak to that follower. Under such a configuration the check reports 'failed to contact quorum of nodes' and steps down while contact is in fact happening, and leadership cannot be retained.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the leader contacts followers at least as often as the lease window for every validated configuration, if some other mechanism refreshes the per-follower contact record on that cadence, or if validation rejects a lease shorter than the contact cadence. An executed witness would be a three-node cluster configured with a heartbeat timeout of a second and a lease of five milliseconds, observing repeated leadership steps down and no sustained leader.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); the churn was not exercised.

The contact cadence also depends on the commit timeout and on round-trip latency, so the exact threshold below which a lease mis-fires is deployment-dependent; the claim is that validation admits leases below any such threshold.
Nothing here concerns the default configuration, whose lease is half the heartbeat timeout and is therefore well above the cadence.

investigations.question: Which peers can supply the acknowledgements that make VerifyLeader succeed, and do they have to be voters?
investigations.hypothesis: The verification threshold is a majority of the voters, but the evidence is not restricted to voters: the leader registers the pending verification with every replication state, replication state exists for every configured peer except the local one regardless of suffrage, and the vote counter records a vote per acknowledgement without any check of who supplied it. A leader that is unreachable from every voter but still reachable from non-voters can therefore satisfy the voter-majority threshold, so a successful verification is not evidence that a quorum of voters is reachable.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the pending verification is registered only with replication states belonging to voters, if votes from non-voters are discarded, or if the threshold is computed over all peers rather than voters. An executed witness would be a cluster with a small voter set and at least two non-voters where the leader is isolated from all voters but kept connected to the non-voters, followed by a verification that succeeds with zero voter acknowledgements.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no isolation was exercised.

The impact on stale reads is bounded by the leadership-lease check, which does count voters only and ends the leader state within the lease, so the gap is exploitable only inside that window; the finding is about the evidence the verification rests on, not about an unbounded stale window.
Only configurations containing non-voters are affected; with every member a voter the two mechanisms agree.

investigations.question: How does a leader learn that a peer has moved to a higher term, given that the heartbeat path does not compare the response term?
investigations.hypothesis: Discovery does not depend on the heartbeat path. The replication loop re-probes every peer with an AppendEntries on a commit-timeout cadence and checks the response term there, stopping that peer's replication and signalling the leader to step down when a higher term appears; the pipelined response path checks the same thing. The heartbeat's success branch only refreshes the contact time and submits acknowledgements to pending verifications, so a higher term it observes is surfaced only when a verification happens to be pending.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the periodic probe can be skipped for a peer (for example a peer whose replication loop is idle or stopped), if the heartbeat response term is compared somewhere not read here, or if the commit-timeout trigger does not send a request every interval. An executed witness would be a peer with a higher term reachable only by heartbeats, observing when the leader steps down.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no such peer was constructed.

The bound on discovery latency is the commit-timeout interval, which the configuration validation only floors at a millisecond, so an operator can choose a large value; that is a tuning consideration noted here rather than a separate finding.
Replication is stopped for a peer once a higher term is seen, so rediscovery after a step-down relies on the new term's leader setup rather than on the old leader's loop.

investigations.question: Do the retained verification tests exercise a configuration containing non-voting members, so that they could constrain which peers may supply the acknowledgements?
investigations.hypothesis: No. The retained verification tests use clusters whose members are all voters: a three-node success case, a single-node case that takes the quorum-of-one shortcut, a two-node case where a follower is forced to a higher term and the verification must fail with a leadership error, and a three-node partial-connect case that disconnects one follower and expects success because the leader plus the remaining voter still meet the voter quorum. The membership tests that add non-voters do not verify leadership, so nothing in the retained suite exercises acknowledgements from a non-voter.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if any retained test adds a non-voting member and then calls VerifyLeader, or asserts a peer-count requirement that excludes non-voters. The partial-connect case is the closest, and it is informative in the opposite direction: it fixes the expectation that one unreachable member in a three-voter cluster still yields success, i.e. that acknowledgements are counted up to the voter quorum rather than requiring unanimity.
limitations: A coverage claim: absence of a test does not establish the behaviour of the uncovered path.
Only the retained test files were searched for verification and non-voter usages.

investigations.question: Can a pooled connection deliver a response that belongs to an earlier request, so that a caller interprets another operation's result as its own?
investigations.hypothesis: No. The synchronous path decodes the receiver's error slot and then the response body before deciding whether the connection may be reused; any decode failure closes the connection instead of pooling it; the pool is keyed by the address actually contacted and bounded; and the two paths whose bodies are streamed rather than framed - install snapshot and the pipelined append stream - hold their own connection and close it rather than returning it to the pool. A connection therefore returns to the pool only when the exchange it was used for has been fully consumed.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if a connection is pooled before the response is fully decoded, if a pooled connection is handed out while a previous exchange is incomplete, or if a streamed body can leave unread bytes on a connection that is then reused. An executed witness would be interleaved RPCs on one address with a truncated or malformed response, observing a later caller reading the earlier response.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no malformed-response scenario was exercised.

The guarantee assumes the wire format is symmetric - exactly one error slot plus one body per response - which holds for the encoding used but is a protocol-level precondition rather than a property of the pool.
Only the default network transport was read; other transports are outside this record.

investigations.question: Which leader-lease values do the retained tests configure relative to the leader's contact cadence, and does any test pin the validation of that relationship?
investigations.hypothesis: Every retained configuration keeps the lease at or above ten times the leader's contact cadence: the shared test configuration uses a fifty-millisecond lease with a fifty-millisecond heartbeat timeout and a five-millisecond commit timeout, one snapshot test raises the heartbeat, election and lease timeouts together to five hundred milliseconds, and a reload test uses a forty-millisecond lease with a fifty-millisecond heartbeat timeout. The lease expectation that exists is the opposite direction - a test disconnects a follower and requires the leader to step down within twice the lease - and the configuration validation test exercises only one invalid field (a snapshot interval below its floor), not the lease relationships.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if a retained test configures a lease below the contact cadence and asserts that leadership is retained, or if a retained test asserts that such a lease is rejected at validation. Reading the configurations and the assertions settles it.
limitations: Coverage claim only; a suite that never chooses a short lease neither confirms nor refutes the mechanism recorded separately.
The cadence figures are derived from the configured heartbeat and commit timeouts rather than measured.

investigations.question: Which admission checks does the heartbeat fast path apply compared with the general RPC path, and what does the difference admit?
investigations.hypothesis: The general path validates the message's protocol version before dispatching and rejects anything outside the supported window, including peers more than one version behind; the heartbeat fast path checks only that the instance is running and that the command is an AppendEntries request, so a heartbeat from a peer this node would reject on any other message is still processed - it can raise the receiver's term, be recorded as leader and refresh the contact record. A follower in that position therefore keeps a leader it cannot replicate from, because every entry-bearing message from that peer is rejected at admission, and it does not start an election because contact keeps being refreshed. The path's doc comment also says it must only be called from the main thread, which contradicts both the registration comment requiring it to be safe concurrently with a blocking RPC and the transport that invokes it on a connection goroutine.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the fast path is only reachable for peers that also pass the general check, if the transport applies the version check before classifying a request as a heartbeat, or if the skipped check could not change any receiver state. An executed witness would be a receiver configured for the current protocol version with a peer more than one version behind acting as leader: observe its heartbeats honoured while its entry-bearing messages are refused at admission.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no mixed-version cluster was run.
The scenario needs a version mix the library documents as unsupported (its policy supports one version back), so the practical severity is bounded by that.
The concurrency comment mismatch does not by itself make the path unsafe: the earlier record shows the safety comes from the transport's zero-field classification of heartbeats.

investigations.question: Can the file snapshot store expose a partially written snapshot, and can its retention delete a snapshot the leader still needs?
investigations.hypothesis: No on both counts. A snapshot is written into a temporary directory whose name is skipped by every listing, the metadata is written inside that directory and synced, and only then is the directory renamed into its final name with the parent directory synced - so a crash leaves either a skipped temporary directory or a complete published snapshot, never a listed-but-incomplete one. Listings sort newest first by term then index and ignore temporary directories and entries without readable, supported metadata; retention keeps the first entries of that newest-first order and deletes the rest; and the constructor refuses a retention below one, so the store cannot be configured to delete everything it publishes.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if a directory becomes visible with its final name before its metadata is durable, if retention iterates the list in oldest-first order, if the constructor accepts a retention of zero, or if a listing can return a directory whose metadata is missing. An executed witness would be a crash at each step of the publish sequence followed by a listing.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no crash-injection was performed.

The order of the listing is by term and then index; for a single node's own snapshots both increase together, so that order equals newest-first, but a store shared out of band between nodes could present a different interleaving.
A failure while reaping is surfaced to the caller as a failure of the snapshot it just published, which is noted as a wart rather than a defect.

investigations.question: Is the factor that scales the snapshot streaming deadline reachable from the transport configuration, and what does a caller have to do instead?
investigations.hypothesis: No. The configuration's timeout documentation says the install-snapshot deadline is multiplied by the snapshot size divided by a named factor, but the configuration struct declares no such field; the factor exists only as an exported field on the transport itself, and the constructor overwrites that field with the package default, so the shipped scaling is a constant unless a caller mutates the live transport. The only configuration-level way to lengthen the snapshot deadline is to raise the transport timeout, which also lengthens the deadline for every other RPC.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the configuration struct (or a sibling constructor) carries the factor, if the constructor preserves a caller-supplied value, or if the scaling site reads something other than the transport field. An executed witness would be a caller setting the documented name in the configuration and observing no change in the snapshot deadline.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no deadline was measured.

The exported transport field can be set after construction, so the scaling is tunable in principle; the finding concerns the documented configuration surface and the timing of such a mutation, not the impossibility of tuning.
Severity is operational: the effect is on how long a snapshot transfer may take before the deadline fires, not on protocol correctness.

investigations.question: After a follower truncates a conflicting suffix and then fails to store the replacement entries, what state is left behind, and does any path correct it?
investigations.hypothesis: The failure path returns without updating the cached last log while the truncation has already removed the suffix, so the cache can point past the store's high index; the repository acknowledges exactly that in a comment. It is nevertheless self-correcting: the previous-log check falls back to the log store whenever the requested index differs from the cached last index, so the next append attempt is evaluated against what the store actually holds, and a successful store of new entries sets the cached position from their last entry.
investigations.discriminator: Refuted if the failure path leaves a state in which the follower can no longer be repaired (for example a cached position that makes every subsequent previous-log check consult only the cache), or if a successful store does not update the cache. An executed witness would be a log store that fails one write after a truncation, followed by a successful retry, checking that the follower's advertised and cached position match the store afterwards.
limitations: Source-only (this run's experiment capacity is exhausted); no failing store was injected.
The self-healing argument assumes the leader retries, which the back-off does; a permanently failing store leaves the follower behind for as long as it fails, which is the fault's own consequence.
The acknowledgement is a comment, not a specification; it is recorded as evidence of awareness rather than as a contract.

investigations.question: Which recorded source-derived findings still lack an executed witness, and what is the smallest execution that would settle each?
investigations.hypothesis: Five recorded findings share the same missing piece, and each can be settled by a small in-memory cluster: (1) the verification evidence gap - a cluster with few voters and at least two non-voters where the leader is isolated from every voter but keeps non-voters connected, observing a successful verification with zero voter acknowledgements; (2) the explicit non-voter transfer - three voters plus one non-voting member, calling the explicit transfer entry point with that member and observing the incumbent lose leadership, the target never win, and the future report success; (3) the transfer readiness cursor - electing a leader while one voter is unreachable, then calling the explicit transfer for that voter immediately on its return and observing TimeoutNow sent before any successful replication response from it; (4) the lease validation gap - a three-node cluster configured with a one-second heartbeat timeout and a five-millisecond lease, observing repeated leadership loss with no sustained leader; (5) the snapshot-install cycle - a leader whose log is compacted above a divergence point and a follower whose cached last index exceeds the leader's snapshot index, observing repeated snapshot transfers with the peer's match index pinned.
investigations.discriminator: Each item is settled by the observation named inside it; a run that cannot execute should leave the item here rather than convert it into a claim. Items 1 to 4 are self-contained in-memory clusters; item 5 additionally needs the follower's log and cached index arranged as its recorded conditions describe, which the existing test helpers can do only partially, so it may need a purpose-built prefix.
limitations: This record adds no source evidence; it consolidates existing discriminators for reuse.
The items are ordered by how self-contained their execution is, not by severity.
Nothing here asserts that any item will be confirmed; several could be refuted by execution, which is the point of listing them.
resume_conditions: A successor run with execution capacity and the same captured snapshot, able to build in-memory clusters in the package under test.
For item 5, either a helper that can seed a follower's log and cached position, or a purpose-built prefix that reaches the state through real messages.
For the previously paused pre-vote fallback question, the counterpart version's transport error text, which no execution in this snapshot can supply.

- *Voter*: a server whose vote is counted in elections and whose match index is used in advancing the leader's commit index.
 - *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

Each server will track two configurations:
 1. its *committed configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot that has been committed, along with its index.
 2. its *latest configuration*: the latest configuration in the log/snapshot (may be committed or uncommitted), along with its index.

When there's no membership change happening, these two will be the same. The latest configuration is almost always the one used, except:
 - When followers truncate the suffix of their logs, they may need to fall back to the committed configuration.
 - When snapshotting, the committed configuration is written, to correspond with the committed log prefix that is being snapshotted.
